title: Can ChatGPT mark writing?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou of No More Marking asks whether AI can mark student writing as accurately as humans, and argues that the real question is not accuracy but how students respond once they know a machine is marking. She recalls Project Essay Grade in 1968, which was more consistent than individual human markers, and shows why such systems were never adopted: they rewarded proxies like length and could be gamed, as when one 2001 system was fooled by a paragraph repeated 37 times. She then tests ChatGPT. Swapping the names in a Romeo and Juliet essay to pass it off as Great Expectations still earned top marks, so literature marking can be gamed, but swapping cigarettes for mobile phones in a persuasive essay was caught, suggesting it is far harder to fool on pure writing. A trial comparing ChatGPT with Comparative Judgement marks showed a decent correlation. Her conclusion is cautious: opaque AI decisions could create loopholes and wasteful gaming-oriented revision, so No More Marking is building a hybrid model with human judgement supervising the AI, like a pilot alongside the autopilot.
points: Christodoulou's key reframing is that AI marking has always been judged wrongly on consistency, when the decisive issue is how students and teaching adapt once they know what the system rewards.
The 1968 PEG system and the 2001 repeated-paragraph exploit show that reliable machine marking can still be gamed, and that gaming changes what students practise.

Her own ChatGPT tests are a clear contrast: swapping character names fooled it on a literature essay, yet a topic swap in a persuasive essay was spotted, so reliability depends on what is being assessed.
Even a non-gameable AI could push students into memorising hacks to fool it, and its opaque decision-making means loopholes could go undetected if all marking were automated.
Her proposed answer is a hybrid in which human Comparative Judgement supervises the AI, keeping validity, the effect on teaching and learning, ahead of mere efficiency.
quotes: Many early AI systems rewarded the length of an essay, simply because essay length does tend to correlate with essay quality. But of course, correlation is not causation. Once people know the AI is rewarding length, they can start to game the system.
This, essentially, is the problem with AI marking. It’s easy for it to be more consistent than humans, because humans are not great at being consistent.

In a way, the justification for human marking is a bit like the justification for a jury system. It may well be inconsistent and unwieldy and error-prone, but it will have a backbone of common sense that prevents really egregious and absurd decisions.

And this, for me, has always been the challenge of AI marking. It’s not about how well it does the job to begin with. It’s about how students respond when they know their work is being marked by AI, and how the AI then responds to that.

This makes sense given what we know about ChatGPT’s strengths. It has been developed as a language model, and it is phenomenally good at understanding and producing natural language. However, it does make factual errors, particularly about complex content.

But if those essays are being marked by AI, students may end up revising for those exams by trying to memorise hacks and hints that will fool the AI. Even if the AI is not gameable, students may still end up wasting time thinking they can crack the code.

However, what if the AI could be supervised by a human who could stop it doing anything obviously absurd? There is a precedent for this in other complex systems. For example, a lot of planes have very sophisticated autopilots, but we still need a human pilot on board.
